key_gap: Both sides locked the same deal — reject $2.28 and $2.15, accept $2.02 at H3, $2,424 secured three hours before a 6h market close with hourly-expiring offers and rising prices — and both computed that optimizing on the realized sequence pays ≥ $2,508 (or the $4,200 broker rate). The gap is execution order: the human set a data-anchored aspiration level (≤ $2.05, the 40th percentile of the quoted distribution, below the $2.10 mean) BEFORE the first quote and applied the first-acceptable rule mechanically in one pass, including a deadline-budgeted relaxation rule (≤ $2.15 at H5); the AI first drafted a per-offer verification strategy — its own governance pipeline would have consumed the hour each offer lives — and needed a WHY-stage correction ('verify the rule once, then execute mechanically') to re-route to the same stop.
learning_signal: Under time pressure, satisficing is a decision procedure, not a fallback: set the aspiration level ex ante and anchor it to market data (percentile of the observed distribution, not a round number), apply the first-acceptable rule mechanically, and treat the deadline as the binding constraint — including a pre-stated relaxation rule that widens the bar's slack as the deadline approaches so the worst case stays below the fallback cost. When the decision procedure is a rule, verify the rule once up front and then execute offers without per-offer deliberation gates, because in a market with expiring offers the pipeline's own decision latency is a hidden search cost; compare that latency against the environment's expiry window before choosing any verify-per-offer strategy.
suggested_improvement: Add to HOW a 'search-environment gate' for time-pressured selection tasks: (a) estimate per-draw search cost, offer-expiry window, deadline, and distribution drift before choosing a stopping rule; (b) if offers expire faster than the pipeline's verify-select latency, pre-verify the acceptance rule once, mark per-offer verification as forbidden, and execute mechanically; (c) set the aspiration level from the distribution's percentile (e.g., the 40th), never a round number, and declare a relaxation rule budgeted against the deadline so the worst case is bounded below the fallback.

key_gap: The pure style executed its rule flawlessly — bar ≤ $3.00/unit, reject S1 at $3.15, accept S2 at $2.95, stop, $708,000 locked — and that IS the failure: the bar was a round number set before any market data (the registered weakness, arbitrary aspiration level, operating as designed), and the premise that justifies satisficing (costly, sequential, expiring search) was absent — quotes arrived in parallel by email at zero marginal cost, did not expire, and the deadline was five days past the quote window. A full screen of the same eight quotes finds S6 at $2.62: the early stop cost ($2.95 − $2.62) × 240,000 = $79,200, 11.2% of the contract. The AI ran the search-affordability test (per-quote cost = 0, parallelism = 8, no expiry → VOI of full screening ≫ cost, G-WHY-4 fails) and selected the full-screen minimum, computing the delta explicitly.
learning_signal: Satisficing has a validity condition: it is rational only when search is costly or expiring. Before applying a first-acceptable rule, run the search-affordability test — per-draw cost, parallelism, expiry, deadline slack; when marginal search cost ≈ 0 (parallel, free, non-expiring quotes), the first-acceptable rule is dominated by a full screen and the aspiration level is arbitrary by construction, with round-number anchors as the most dangerous case. Anchor aspiration levels to observed evidence when free observation exists (screen the market, then set the bar), and treat 'the bar was met' as an invalid stopping justification in zero-cost search environments.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'search-affordability gate' to WHY, before any stopping rule is adopted: (a) enumerate search cost (per-draw cost, parallelism, expiry, deadline slack) and compute VOI of full screening (expected spread × volume vs cost); (b) if marginal search cost ≈ 0, mandate full screening and select the optimum, forbidding first-acceptable stops; (c) if search is costly or expiring, apply aspiration-level stopping — but anchor the bar to observed distribution percentiles and add a deadline-budgeted relaxation rule; (d) flag round-number aspiration levels set before data as suspect and require an anchor before accepting them.
